title: What can you say about cranberry in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 1 wording for cranberry; the strongest is "Provides antioxidants that help protect cells against free radical damage" (moderate, up to 30 g fresh fruit a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Prevents or treats urinary tract infections (UTIs), outside FDA's qualified wording".

supported_wordings.wording: Provides antioxidants that help protect cells against free radical damage.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it at up to 30 g of fresh fruit a day; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: up to 30 g fresh fruit a day
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults 18 and older. Health Canada: not more than 30 g of fresh fruit a day (about 4-5 g dried fruit), or not more than 950 ml of juice.
supported_wordings.form: Fresh, dried or powdered fruit, counted as fresh fruit

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Prevents or treats urinary tract infections (UTIs), outside FDA's qualified wording
wordings_to_avoid.why: Names a disease. FDA's qualified claim for cranberry dietary supplements has set wording and conditions (see fda_health_claims).

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Works like an antibiotic for bladder infections
wordings_to_avoid.why: Presents the product as a drug.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

sources.name: FDA qualified health claim: Cranberry dietary supplements and recurrent urinary tract infection in healthy women

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
